title: Deepest Bracket Level in a Formula
statement:
A spreadsheet cell holds a well-formed arithmetic formula s made of single digits, the operators + - * /, and round brackets. Every bracket is matched.

The depth of a position is how many bracket pairs enclose it. Return the largest depth anywhere in the formula. A formula without brackets has depth 0.

examples.why: The 3 and the 1 sit inside two pairs of brackets: the outer one starting after 7* and the inner one around 3-1.
There are three bracket pairs in total, but the deepest point, the 5, is only inside two of them. Count nesting, not pairs.

constraints: s is a valid formula with matched brackets
hints: Walk the formula left to right. What single number tells you how deep you are right now?
An opening bracket takes you one level deeper; a closing bracket brings you one level back up. Everything else leaves the depth alone.
Keep a counter for the current depth and remember the largest value it ever reaches. You do not need an actual stack, because the brackets are guaranteed to match.

explain.intuition:
The usual tool for brackets is a stack: push on (, pop on ). Here the stack's contents never matter, only its height, and the height at any moment is exactly the depth of that position. So replace the stack with a counter: +1 on (, −1 on ).

The answer is the highest the counter ever gets. It is the same thing as finding the deepest nesting level of elements in a serialized DOM tree by counting open and close tags.
steps: For each character: on (, add 1 to depth and update best.
pitfalls: Counting bracket pairs instead of nesting. (1)+(2)+(3) has three pairs but depth 1.
Updating best after a closing bracket instead of after an opening one, which reports one level too few.

solutions.title: Depth of every position from scratch
solutions.idea: For each position, count the opening minus closing brackets before it. The largest such count is the answer.

solutions.title: One running counter
solutions.idea: The stack height is all that matters, so keep it as a number: +1 on an opening bracket, −1 on a closing one, and track the maximum.

followups: The brackets might not be balanced. Return -1 in that case, still in one pass.
The formula also uses [ ] and { }, and they must nest correctly. Now you need a real stack. Why?
